implementation_notes: Swift implements the pattern in the language: writing any P makes the type an existential that stores any conforming value behind an inline buffer (three words on 64-bit platforms) with a heap fallback, plus a witness table for the protocol's methods, so [any Shape] holds unrelated conformers and dispatch is dynamic; the documentation states that boxed protocol types do not preserve type identity. Since Swift 5.7 existentials also work for protocols with associated types, with the SE-0309 caveat that the existential does not itself conform to the protocol, so requirements involving Self or an associated type stay uncallable. Prefer some P (opaque) or generics when only one concrete type is involved - opaque types keep type identity, avoid the box and let the compiler specialize - and fall back to the manual closure-box eraser when the existential cannot express the contract.
pitfalls: Existentials box: values larger than the inline buffer are heap-allocated and every call goes through the witness table plus dynamic exclusivity checks, so they are the wrong choice in hot loops - use generics or some P at API boundaries.

An existential does not conform to its own protocol: any P cannot satisfy a generic P constraint or an associated-type requirement (for example Equatable's Self-based ==), so such operations must be avoided or type-erased by hand.

any is optional in the Swift 5 language mode (SE-0335 introduced it and Swift 6 still does not require it), so older code mixed existentials with generics silently - enable -enable-upcoming-feature ExistentialAny to surface them.

variants.name: Closure-box type eraser (the AnyView/AnyPublisher pattern)
variants.idiom_name: struct AnyX: P storing closures captured over the concrete value
variants.implementation_notes: When the existential cannot be used - pre-5.7 toolchains, protocols whose associated types or Self requirements make any P unusable, or performance-sensitive boundaries - the standard library's own trick is reproduced by hand: a concrete struct that conforms to the protocol and stores closures capturing the concrete value, reproducing a witness table with controllable dispatch points. This is exactly the shape of AnyView, AnySequence and AnyPublisher. It preserves value semantics, avoids the existential container, but pays closure indirection and reference counting, and erases only the operations it exposes.
pitfalls: Only the erased operations exist: every additional protocol requirement needs its own stored closure, so extending the protocol silently narrows the eraser's conformance.

The closures capture the concrete value; when it is a reference type the eraser shares it (reference semantics leak through a value type), and a retained capture can form a cycle if the eraser is stored back into the captured object.
